query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Machine-learning models trained on existing thermodynamic and structural data can accurately and efficiently predict melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the high-entropy-alloy (HEA) family, outperforming traditional CALPHAD and rule-of-mixtures approaches in both speed and accuracy for unexplored compositions.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) in solid phase, with known composition and structure.
generation.intervention: Application of machine-learning models (e.g., neural networks, random forests) trained on curated thermodynamic databases and structural descriptors to predict fusion and liquid-phase properties.
generation.conditions: Predictions made for HEAs with compositions within the range of training data (typically 3–7 principal elements, equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios), under ambient pressure and standard melting conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale descriptors (e.g., atomic radii, electronegativity, mixing entropy, lattice distortion) and compositional features serve as input mediators for the model.
generation.mechanism: The ML model learns nonlinear correlations between structural/compositional features and thermodynamic properties, leveraging patterns in existing experimental and computational data to generalize predictions for new HEA compositions.
generation.predicted_outcome: For HEAs within the training domain, predicted melting temperatures will have mean absolute errors (MAE) below 50 K, enthalpy and entropy of fusion errors below 10%, and volume change at melting errors below 10% compared to experimental values. Liquid-phase thermodynamic properties (e.g., heat capacity, viscosity) will be predicted within 15% error. Prediction speed will be orders of magnitude faster than first-principles or CALPHAD calculations.
generation.baseline: Traditional CALPHAD and rule-of-mixtures approaches, which typically yield larger errors (MAE > 100 K for melting temperature, >15% for fusion properties) and require more computational time for each composition.
generation.boundary: Applicability is limited to HEAs with compositions and structural types represented in the training data; extrapolation to radically different compositions or phases (e.g., intermetallics, amorphous alloys) may yield unreliable predictions.
generation.uncertainty: Accuracy depends on the quality and diversity of training data; for compositions far from the training domain, uncertainty increases and predictions may be unreliable. Liquid-phase properties are less well-represented in existing databases, increasing uncertainty for these predictions.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a set of HEA compositions not present in the training data. Measure melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties experimentally. Compare ML model predictions to experimental results and to CALPHAD predictions.
measurements: Volume change at melting (dilatometry or X-ray)
Liquid-phase heat capacity and viscosity (high-temperature calorimetry and rheometry)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML model's predictions for any property have mean absolute errors greater than those of CALPHAD or rule-of-mixtures approaches (e.g., >100 K for melting temperature, >15% for fusion properties) for the test set, the hypothesis is falsified.
